title: Bigs Who Pass or Shoot Threes
brief: Which big men add assists or threes on top of rebounds and blocks, giving rare category combinations? It must explain why combining categories that do not usually go together carries extra value in H2H.
summary: Big men who add assists or threes to rebounds and blocks matter more in our 9-cat H2H league, because they cover categories that usually come from guards. The catch is that threes and FG% pull against each other. A big who drifts out to the arc can lose offensive rebounds and rim finishing, so pay for the combination only when his FG% still holds up.

paragraphs.text: The experts say players who combine categories that do not usually go together carry extra value. Rebounds plus assists is the example they give. In our league each week is nine separate contests against one opponent. Most rosters get rebounds and blocks from bigs, and assists and threes from guards. A big who also brings assists or threes covers a category from a slot that normally gives nothing there.

That frees the rest of your roster. If your C slot already adds assists or threes, your G and Util slots can chase steals, FT% or low turnovers. With only 12 drafted players per team and 10 starters, one player who covers an extra category is worth more than his raw totals suggest.
The experts call one version a fantasy cheat code: a big man with blocks, threes, rebounds and a good field goal percentage. Few players give all four, and that is why the profile is worth chasing.

sections.heading: The price of threes from a big

paragraphs.text: A center who takes more threes plays farther from the rim. His offensive rebounds and rim finishing tend to drop. His assists and three-point attempts tend to go up. So threes and assists from a big often arrive together, but some rebounds and FG% can leave at the same time.

The experts do not fully agree on how often this works. One view is that a big with blocks, threes, rebounds and good FG% is a cheat code worth building around. The other is that threes and FG% pull against each other, so adding threes to a big man build is hard and often costs you FG%. Both can be true. The full profile is very strong, but it is rare, and most stretch bigs give you the threes with a weaker FG%.

sections.heading: How to use this in our auction

paragraphs.text: Before you bid on any big, list what he adds beyond rebounds and blocks. Give extra value to assists or threes only if his FG% is still good. FG% is a team ratio, so a high-volume big with a poor percentage hurts it more than a low-volume guard does.

If you buy a big whose threes come with a weak FG%, plan the rest of the roster around it. Either add a high-FG% rim big in a Util slot, or commit to a punt FG% build and stop paying for FG% elsewhere. Do not pay for the threes and then also bid on FG% help you cannot use.
Assist bigs follow the same logic for guards. If your center gives real assists, you can spend less on pass-first guards and use those dollars on threes or steals.

sections.heading: What to check in the first weeks

paragraphs.text: For every big you own with threes or assists, track three numbers in the first two to three weeks: three-point attempts, offensive rebounds and FG%. If his three-point attempts climb while his rebounds and FG% slide, that is the pattern the notes describe. Decide early whether his threes and assists still beat what a rim big would give you.

Use FAB and your 6 weekly adds to fix whatever the combination costs you. If your stretch big is dragging FG%, pick up a rim-running big. If he is giving you threes and assists as hoped, you can drop a guard who only gave you those same categories.
